- introduce a documented high - level api for session shutdown that supports a configurable grace period ( e. g., streamwithgrace ( ctx, grace time. duration ) ). - when parent context is canceled, sdk will attempt to drain in - flight responses and send a clean end - of - stream signal within the grace period ; if grace expires, session closes and returns context. canceled to caller. - reconnect policy exposed via options : retrynever | retryimmediate | retrywithbackoff ( with jitter ). default : retrywithbackoff for transient network errors, no retry for server - initiated rejections ( 4xx ). - no breaking changes to

Minor version bumps for all SDKs.\",\n  \"description\": \"Context: Teams reported subtle production flakes where long-running streaming sessions would deadlock while the SDK attempted token refresh near connection shutdown. Root cause: mismatched defaults across languages (py: grace=5s, ts: grace=2s, go: none) combined with non-deterministic drain logic in the stream consumer. Motivation: provide predictable, cross-language semantics for credential grace windows and give app authors explicit, ergonomic controls for draining streaming responses. What this PR does: 1) introduce a unified config property 'session_grace_ms' (default 5000) surface on all SDK clients; SDKs continue to accept language-idiomatic names but map to the canonical value in shared test fixtures. 2) add 'stream_drain_timeout_ms' with a default of 3000 to guard shutdown path; streaming helpers now expose drain_until_eof(timeout_ms) convenience methods on Python/TS and DrainWithContext(ctx, timeoutMs) on Go. 3) refactor token refresh handshake to be cancelable and cooperative with drain: refresh now registers a short-lived lease and yields shutdown precedence to drain paths. 4) add cross-sdk integration tests that simulate concurrent refresh and EOF arrival, and a stress test harness that reproduces the original deadlock pattern. 5) bump package versions: python 1.9.0, typescript 2.6.1, go 1.4.0 (minor/patch bumps only). Checklist: - [x] design doc (ENG-1842) and UX doc reviewed - [x] unit tests added for all three SDKs - [x] crosslang integration test added to perf lab - [x] reviewed and approved by SDK leads - [x] release notes drafted Testing and CI: initial CI run showed a flaky TS streaming test (stream-drain-signal) \\u2014 reproduced locally, fixed race by moving the drain signal to the top-level loop and adding a short backoff in the TS connector. All CI checks green on rerun. Migration notes: default values are conservative; existing callers should be unaffected. If teams relied on the previous lower grace intervals, they can set session_grace_ms explicitly. Operational notes: this change reduces rare stalled streams at the cost of a modestly longer shutdown window in some workloads; metrics added to the Console: sdk.session.grace_ms_applied and sdk.stream.drain_timeout_ms_applied. Rollout plan: quick canary to ~10% of hosted SDK traffic for 48h, then gradual increase. If we see an uptick in shutdown latency beyond expectations, we will roll back and revert to per-sdk defaults while we iterate. Related: SUP-4021 (customer incident), ENG-1842 design doc.\",\n  \"commits\": [\n    \"a1c3e9b: design + initial python impl for session_grace and drain helper\",\n    \"b7f4d22: ts connector: expose drainUntilEof and wire session_grace mapping\",\n    \"c2e8f00: go: add DrainWithContext and opt-in session_grace config\",\n    \"d4f1a55: cross-sdk tests: concurrent-refresh-and-eof harness\",\n    \"e8b3c41: fix(ts): race in stream-drain-signal backoff\",\n    \"f1a2b33: bump versions and update changelogs\"\n  ],\n  \"files_changed\": [\n    \"sdk/python/redwood_client/session.py\",\n    \"sdk/python/tests/test_stream_drain.py\",\n    \"sdk/typescript/src/stream/connector.ts\",\n    \"sdk/typescript/tests/stream_drain.test.ts\",\n    \"sdk/go/stream/drain.go\",\n    \"sdk/go/stream/drain_test.go\",\n    \"sdk/common/config/session_defaults.go\",\n    \"perf/bench/stream_deadlock_repro/README.md\",\n    \"perf/bench/stream_deadlock_repro/harness.py\",\n    \"docs/sdk/session_and_streaming.md\",\n    \"packages/python/CHANGELOG.md\",\n    \"packages/typescript/CHANGELOG.md\"\n  ],\n  \"review_comments\": [\n    \"Omar Reyes: Can you explain why 5s was chosen as the default? Is it empirically driven?\",\n    \"Ava Chen: Chose 5s after running the stress harness under realistic network jitter; it covered 99.7% of reproductions while keeping shutdown latency acceptable. Added note in UX doc.\",\n    \"Nina Patel: TS test was flaky in CI \\u2014 I see you added the backoff, please add a short comment explaining the tradeoff so it's not removed by future authors.\",\n    \"Ava Chen: Added inline comment and extracted backoff as 'drainYieldBackoffMs' constant with a unit test asserting > 95% success over 500 runs.\",\n    \"Soren Li: Approve after the changelog bump. Observability: can we emit a metric when refresh yields to drain?\",\n    \"Ava Chen: Added metric sdk.refresh.yield_to_drain with counts and labels (sdk_lang, client_id).\"\n  ],\n  \"ci_checks\": [\n    \"unit:python - passed (34s)\",\n    \"unit:typescript - failed (flaky stream-drain-signal) then passed on rerun (timeout fix) (1m12s)\",\n    \"unit:go - passed (28s)\",\n    \"integration:cross-sdk - passed (6m8s)\",\n    \"lint - passed\",\n    \"e2e:perf-harness - passed (2m30s)\"\n  ],\n  \"merge\": \"squash and merge by Nina Patel. Commit message: 'unify(session): align session_grace and stream drain across SDKs; add ergonomics and tests'\",\n  \"notes_for_backport\": \"Backport to release/1.9.x (python) and release/2.6.x (typescript) recommended if teams want immediate fix in older branches; go change is non-breaking and can be cherry-picked.\",\n  \"manual_steps\": \"After deploy: watch sdk.session.grace_ms_applied and sdk.stream.drain_timeout_ms_applied in Console for anomalies; if shutdown latency rises, temporarily set session_grace_ms to previous per-sdk value and open support ticket.\",\n  \"changelog_entries\": [\n    \"python: v1.9.0 - Add session_grace_ms and stream drain_until_eof helper; stability fixes for concurrent refresh/drain.\",\n    \"typescript: v2.6.1 - Expose drainUntilEof(timeoutMs) and align session grace defaults; fix race in stream-drain signal.\",\n    \"go: v1.4.0 - Add DrainWithContext and session_grace option; improved shutdown behavior during refresh.\"\n  ],\n  \"original_location\": \"github/redwood/pr-405999-unify-session-grace-and-stream-drain-crosssdk.json\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"release_notes\",\n    \"review_comments\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_25fbc8050fe94a8c848df35be7b65f78\"\n}",

{
  "repo": "redwood",
  "pr_number": "405999",
  "title": "unify-session-grace-and-stream-drain-crosssdk",
  "author": "Ava Chen",
  "created_at": "2026-02-15",
  "updated_at": "2026-02-28",
  "merged_at": "2026-02-28",
  "state": "merged",
  "base_branch": "main",
  "head_branch": "feature/sync-cred-grace-stream-drain-crosssdk",
  "reviewers": [
    "Omar Reyes",
    "Nina Patel",
    "Soren Li"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "sdk",
    "cross-sdk",
    "auth",
    "streaming",
    "ergonomics",
    "perf"
  ],
  "linked_linear": [
    "ENG-1842",
    "ENG-1890"
  ],
  "linked_jira": [
    "SUP-4021"
  ],
  "ci_status": "pass",
  "files_changed_count": "12",
  "additions": "265",
  "deletions": "112",
  "breaking_change": "false",
  "release_notes": "Aligned session grace/reauth defaults across Python/TS/Go SDKs, added ergonomic stream drain helpers, fixed an edge case that could cause stalled drains when token refresh overlaps generation. Minor version bumps for all SDKs.",
  "description": "Context: Teams reported subtle production flakes where long-running streaming sessions would deadlock while the SDK attempted token refresh near connection shutdown. Root cause: mismatched defaults across languages (py: grace=5s, ts: grace=2s, go: none) combined with non-deterministic drain logic in the stream consumer. Motivation: provide predictable, cross-language semantics for credential grace windows and give app authors explicit, ergonomic controls for draining streaming responses. What this PR does: 1) introduce a unified config property 'session_grace_ms' (default 5000) surface on all SDK clients; SDKs continue to accept language-idiomatic names but map to the canonical value in shared test fixtures. 2) add 'stream_drain_timeout_ms' with a default of 3000 to guard shutdown path; streaming helpers now expose drain_until_eof(timeout_ms) convenience methods on Python/TS and DrainWithContext(ctx, timeoutMs) on Go. 3) refactor token refresh handshake to be cancelable and cooperative with drain: refresh now registers a short-lived lease and yields shutdown precedence to drain paths. 4) add cross-sdk integration tests that simulate concurrent refresh and EOF arrival, and a stress test harness that reproduces the original deadlock pattern. 5) bump package versions: python 1.9.0, typescript 2.6.1, go 1.4.0 (minor/patch bumps only). Checklist: - [x] design doc (ENG-1842) and UX doc reviewed - [x] unit tests added for all three SDKs - [x] crosslang integration test added to perf lab - [x] reviewed and approved by SDK leads - [x] release notes drafted Testing and CI: initial CI run showed a flaky TS streaming test (stream-drain-signal) \u2014 reproduced locally, fixed race by moving the drain signal to the top-level loop and adding a short backoff in the TS connector. All CI checks green on rerun. Migration notes: default values are conservative; existing callers should be unaffected. If teams relied on the previous lower grace intervals, they can set session_grace_ms explicitly. Operational notes: this change reduces rare stalled streams at the cost of a modestly longer shutdown window in some workloads; metrics added to the Console: sdk.session.grace_ms_applied and sdk.stream.drain_timeout_ms_applied. Rollout plan: quick canary to ~10% of hosted SDK traffic for 48h, then gradual increase. If we see an uptick in shutdown latency beyond expectations, we will roll back and revert to per-sdk defaults while we iterate. Related: SUP-4021 (customer incident), ENG-1842 design doc.",
  "commits": [
    "a1c3e9b: design + initial python impl for session_grace and drain helper",
    "b7f4d22: ts connector: expose drainUntilEof and wire session_grace mapping",
    "c2e8f00: go: add DrainWithContext and opt-in session_grace config",
    "d4f1a55: cross-sdk tests: concurrent-refresh-and-eof harness",
    "e8b3c41: fix(ts): race in stream-drain-signal backoff",
    "f1a2b33: bump versions and update changelogs"
  ],
  "files_changed": [
    "sdk/python/redwood_client/session.py",
    "sdk/python/tests/test_stream_drain.py",
    "sdk/typescript/src/stream/connector.ts",
    "sdk/typescript/tests/stream_drain.test.ts",
    "sdk/go/stream/drain.go",
    "sdk/go/stream/drain_test.go",
    "sdk/common/config/session_defaults.go",
    "perf/bench/stream_deadlock_repro/README.md",
    "perf/bench/stream_deadlock_repro/harness.py",
    "docs/sdk/session_and_streaming.md",
    "packages/python/CHANGELOG.md",
    "packages/typescript/CHANGELOG.md"
  ],
  "review_comments": [
    "Omar Reyes: Can you explain why 5s was chosen as the default? Is it empirically driven?",
    "Ava Chen: Chose 5s after running the stress harness under realistic network jitter; it covered 99.7% of reproductions while keeping shutdown latency acceptable. Added note in UX doc.",
    "Nina Patel: TS test was flaky in CI \u2014 I see you added the backoff, please add a short comment explaining the tradeoff so it's not removed by future authors.",
    "Ava Chen: Added inline comment and extracted backoff as 'drainYieldBackoffMs' constant with a unit test asserting > 95% success over 500 runs.",
    "Soren Li: Approve after the changelog bump. Observability: can we emit a metric when refresh yields to drain?",
    "Ava Chen: Added metric sdk.refresh.yield_to_drain with counts and labels (sdk_lang, client_id)."
  ],
  "ci_checks": [
    "unit:python - passed (34s)",
    "unit:typescript - failed (flaky stream-drain-signal) then passed on rerun (timeout fix) (1m12s)",
    "unit:go - passed (28s)",
    "integration:cross-sdk - passed (6m8s)",
    "lint - passed",
    "e2e:perf-harness - passed (2m30s)"
  ],
  "merge": "squash and merge by Nina Patel. Commit message: 'unify(session): align session_grace and stream drain across SDKs; add ergonomics and tests'",
  "notes_for_backport": "Backport to release/1.9.x (python) and release/2.6.x (typescript) recommended if teams want immediate fix in older branches; go change is non-breaking and can be cherry-picked.",
  "manual_steps": "After deploy: watch sdk.session.grace_ms_applied and sdk.stream.drain_timeout_ms_applied in Console for anomalies; if shutdown latency rises, temporarily set session_grace_ms to previous per-sdk value and open support ticket.",
  "changelog_entries": [
    "python: v1.9.0 - Add session_grace_ms and stream drain_until_eof helper; stability fixes for concurrent refresh/drain.",
    "typescript: v2.6.1 - Expose drainUntilEof(timeoutMs) and align session grace defaults; fix race in stream-drain signal.",
    "go: v1.4.0 - Add DrainWithContext and session_grace option; improved shutdown behavior during refresh."
  ],

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_be54bc0a5c6843699e8c15e9534543e6",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/slack/devex/3412345678-gen-stream-startup-deadlock-repro.json",
    "title": "devex",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/slack",
    "content": "{\n  \"channel\": \"devex\",\n  \"thread_ts\": \"3412345678\",\n  \"first_message_ts\": \"3412345678\",\n  \"last_message_ts\": \"3412345878\",\n  \"participants\": [\n    \"mia\",\n    \"raj\",\n    \"tomas\",\n    \"devex-bot\",\n    \"ci-bot\"\n  ],\n  \"text\": \"mia: Repro for a startup deadlock I hit when the generator stream and auth refresh race.\\nmia: Steps: 1) start generator stream with request ctx 2) mid-stream token rotates 3) client attempts retry/auth refresh and we get a goroutine leak + stream stop responding.\\nmia: Minimal log: \\n```\\n2026-03-23T14:12:03Z generator: start stream id=st-3a2\\n2026-03-23T14:12:04Z auth: refresh started token=shortlived\\n2026-03-23T14:12:05Z generator: write failed err=context canceled\\n2026-03-23T14:12:10Z generator: no further events, goroutines: 8 (stuck in io.Copy)\\n```\\nmia: Example problematic pattern (simplified):\\n```\\nfunc StartStream(ctx context.Context) error {\\n  // reusing request ctx for long-living background ops\\n  go func() {\\n    // auth refresh uses ctx too -> if request ctx canceled, refresh stops\\n    token, err := refreshToken(ctx)\\n    if err != nil { /* ... */ }\\n    _ = token\\n  }()\\n  // long-running generator relying on same ctx\\n  return runGenerator(ctx)\\n}\\n```\\nmia: So when client code cancels the request (deadline or user), auth refresh also stops and the generator's reconnect/retry path stalls.\\nraj: ugh yeah that sounds like ctx bleed. Can you share a short repro repo or a snippet that shows the goroutine counts?\\nmia: I'll paste a small sample app in a sec. The key is we call `client.Generate(ctxWithTimeout, ...)` and inside the SDK we start a background refresh with the same ctx.\\nmia: Repro repo: https://github.com/redwood/repro-stream-deadlock (private) - main.go shows the flow.\\\\n\\nmia: sample main snippet: \\n```\\nfunc main() {\\n  ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second)\\n  defer cancel()\\n  stream, err := client.Generator(ctx, opts)\\n  if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }\\n  // consume stream slowly\\n  for msg := range stream.Chan() {\\n    time.Sleep(800 * time.Millisecond)\\n    fmt.Println(msg)\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n\\ntomas: This is a common pitfall: do not let short-lived request ctx control background maintenance work. Background tasks (auth refresh, reconnect backoff) should use a separate context derived from parent but with their own lifecycle, or be cancellable via explicit Close/Stop API on the stream object.\\ntomas: Suggestion: in SDK, create streamCtx, streamCancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background()) and tie streamCancel to stream.Close(), not to the request ctx. Keep request ctx only for initial handshake.\\ntomas: Example from my notes: \\n```\\n// inside sdk\\nhandshakeCtx := ctx // use request ctx for initial HTTP handshake only\\nstreamCtx, streamCancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())\\ngo func() { // background auth refresher\\n  for {\\n    select {\\n    case <-streamCtx.Done():\\n      return\\n    case <-time.After(refreshInterval):\\n      // use a transient ctx with timeout for refresh so it doesn't inherit request deadline\\n      rctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)\\n      _ = refreshAuth(rctx)\\n      cancel()\\n    }\\n  }\\n}()\\n// link streamCancel to stream.Close()\\n```\\n\\nraj: that matches what we've done elsewhere. Also recommend any retries that mutate connection state be guarded by a single `reconnectMu` so only one goroutine tries to rebuild connections.\\n\\nmia: One wrinkle: when the request ctx expires, app code expects the stream to stop quickly. If stream runs on its own ctx, we should still signal the worker to stop soon after request ctx done. Maybe best UX: stream.Cancel() called by SDK when request ctx canceled, but ensure refresh retries use transient ctxs so they don't block.\\n\\ntomas: Exactly. Two rules: (1) never run long retry loops on the request ctx, (2) make the stream object own its lifecycle and expose a Close/Cancel API so caller can decide.\\n\\nmia: Would an ergonomic API help? e.g., `stream, err := client.GeneratorStream(ctx, opts)` returning `stream` that implements `Close()` and `Err()`; on ctx cancel we call `stream.Close()` internally but allow background transient ops to finish quickly.\\n\\nraj: API sounds good. {
  "channel": "devex",
  "thread_ts": "3412345678",
  "first_message_ts": "3412345678",
  "last_message_ts": "3412345878",
  "participants": [
    "mia",
    "raj",
    "tomas",
    "devex-bot",
    "ci-bot"
  ],
  "text": "mia: Repro for a startup deadlock I hit when the generator stream and auth refresh race.
mia: Steps: 1) start generator stream with request ctx 2) mid-stream token rotates 3) client attempts retry/auth refresh and we get a goroutine leak + stream stop responding.
mia: Minimal log: 
```
2026-03-23T14:12:03Z generator: start stream id=st-3a2
2026-03-23T14:12:04Z auth: refresh started token=shortlived
2026-03-23T14:12:05Z generator: write failed err=context canceled
2026-03-23T14:12:10Z generator: no further events, goroutines: 8 (stuck in io.Copy)
```
mia: Example problematic pattern (simplified):
```
func StartStream(ctx context.Context) error {
  // reusing request ctx for long-living background ops
  go func() {
    // auth refresh uses ctx too -> if request ctx canceled, refresh stops
    token, err := refreshToken(ctx)
    if err != nil { /* ... */ }
    _ = token
  }()
  // long-running generator relying on same ctx
  return runGenerator(ctx)
}
```
mia: So when client code cancels the request (deadline or user), auth refresh also stops and the generator's reconnect/retry path stalls.
raj: ugh yeah that sounds like ctx bleed. Can you share a short repro repo or a snippet that shows the goroutine counts?
mia: I'll paste a small sample app in a sec. The key is we call `client.Generate(ctxWithTimeout, ...)` and inside the SDK we start a background refresh with the same ctx.
mia: Repro repo: https://github.com/redwood/repro-stream-deadlock (private) - main.go shows the flow.\n
mia: sample main snippet: 
```
func main() {
  ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second)
  defer cancel()
  stream, err := client.Generator(ctx, opts)
  if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
  // consume stream slowly
  for msg := range stream.Chan() {
    time.Sleep(800 * time.Millisecond)
    fmt.Println(msg)
  }
}
```

tomas: This is a common pitfall: do not let short-lived request ctx control background maintenance work. Background tasks (auth refresh, reconnect backoff) should use a separate context derived from parent but with their own lifecycle, or be cancellable via explicit Close/Stop API on the stream object.
tomas: Suggestion: in SDK, create streamCtx, streamCancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background()) and tie streamCancel to stream.Close(), not to the request ctx. Keep request ctx only for initial handshake.
tomas: Example from my notes: 
```
// inside sdk
handshakeCtx := ctx // use request ctx for initial HTTP handshake only
streamCtx, streamCancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
go func() { // background auth refresher
  for {
    select {
    case <-streamCtx.Done():
      return
    case <-time.After(refreshInterval):
      // use a transient ctx with timeout for refresh so it doesn't inherit request deadline
      rctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
      _ = refreshAuth(rctx)
      cancel()
    }
  }
}()
// link streamCancel to stream.Close()
```

raj: that matches what we've done elsewhere. Also recommend any retries that mutate connection state be guarded by a single `reconnectMu` so only one goroutine tries to rebuild connections.

mia: One wrinkle: when the request ctx expires, app code expects the stream to stop quickly. If stream runs on its own ctx, we should still signal the worker to stop soon after request ctx done. Maybe best UX: stream.Cancel() called by SDK when request ctx canceled, but ensure refresh retries use transient ctxs so they don't block.

tomas: Exactly. Two rules: (1) never run long retry loops on the request ctx, (2) make the stream object own its lifecycle and expose a Close/Cancel API so caller can decide.

mia: Would an ergonomic API help? e.g., `stream, err := client.GeneratorStream(ctx, opts)` returning `stream` that implements `Close()` and `Err()`; on ctx cancel we call `stream.Close()` internally but allow background transient ops to finish quickly.

raj: API sounds good. Also let's add explicit `tokenSource` abstraction in SDK so refresh is centralized and testable. Tests can fake a slow refresh to assert no leak.

devex-bot: FYI @tomas @raj there's an open issue template for generator ergonomics: https://github.com/redwood/redwood/issues/6752 (please link repro) :information_source:

ci-bot: build/sampleapp (repro-stream-deadlock) failed on integration: `TestStreamCancellation` — flake, captured goroutine dump attached.

mia: I'll open the GH issue with the repro, a small failing test, and attach the goroutine dump. Planning to add a sample app that demonstrates correct pattern using `streamCtx` and transient refresh ctxs.

tomas: If you want I can draft a PR that changes SDK internals to use `streamCtx` + `refreshCtx` pattern and add a small unit test.

mia: That would be amazing, thanks. I'll add steps in the issue for the test and tag you.

raj: leaving a note to ensure we update docs/quickstart to mention that `context` passed into `Generate` is only for handshake and short-lived ops — long-lived background work uses stream-owned contexts. Could prevent a lot of confusion.

mia: Agreed. I'll add a short blurb in dev docs once PR lands.

mia: Thanks all :heart:",

    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Predictive Autoscaling (Dedicated) \\u2014 Known Issues & Recommended Workarounds\",\n  \"space\": \"customer-success-and-support\",\n  \"author\": \"Dev Patel\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"customer-success\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-07-18\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2025-09-05\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Lauren Bishop\",\n    \"Vanessa Ortiz\",\n    \"Rafael Mendes\",\n    \"Allison Grant\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"dedicated\",\n    \"autoscaling\",\n    \"predictive-scaling\",\n    \"known-issues\",\n    \"support-playbook\",\n    \"rollout\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/escalation-playbook/autoscaling-bounds-customer-escalation-playbook.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/dedicated-autoscaler-troubleshooting-runbook.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/autoscaling-bounds-observability-dashboard-spec.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/product-docs/release-notes/dedicated-autoscaling-bounds-and-predictive-mode-release-notes.json\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"body\": \"h1. Overview\\nPredictive autoscaling is an opt-in mode for *Redwood Dedicated* that biases scale decisions using forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical request rates/latency). Predictive mode *does not* override customer-configured *min/max bounds* and will fall back to reactive signals when forecasts are stale/unavailable.\\n\\nThis page lists the most common *known issues* observed during pilot/canary, how to recognize them, and recommended *workarounds* for Customer Success and Support. This is not a full runbook; for deep debugging and mitigations, use the dedicated on-call runbook linked above.\\n\\nh2. Scope / When this page applies\\n* Applies to:* Dedicated deployments with predictive mode enabled (feature-flagged per account/deployment).\\n* Not applicable to:* Hosted API autoscaling or Dedicated deployments running reactive-only scaling.\\n\\nh2. Quick definitions (customer-friendly)\\n* *Forecast / prediction:* A projected target capacity (replicas/GPU slices) for an upcoming time window.\\n* *Reactive scaling:* Signals like queue depth, saturation, and latency that trigger scaling based on current conditions.\\n* *Bounds:* Customer-configured *min* and *max* capacity. The autoscaler clamps desired capacity within these bounds.\\n* *Bound-hit:* When the autoscaler wants to go above max or below min but is prevented by bounds.\\n\\nh1. Rollout caveats (read first)\\n1) *Opt-in + guarded rollout:* Predictive mode is still rolling out. Some regions/accounts may not be eligible.\\n2) *Model/workload sensitivity:* Highly bursty workloads with low steady-state traffic can produce noisy forecasts.\\n3) *Do not promise \\u201cno queueing\\u201d under max bounds:* If traffic exceeds max-bound capacity and the region cannot burst, queueing/latency can occur. This is expected behavior; the product surfaces it via bound-hit metrics.\\n4) *Time-to-effect:* Changes to predictive settings may take up to *10\\u201320 minutes* to reflect in decisions (depending on caching and evaluation intervals).\\n\\nh1. Known issues & workarounds\\n\\nh2. 1) False positives (over-scaling before traffic arrives)\\n*Symptoms*\\n* Capacity ramps up early; customer sees increased spend/idle utilization.\\n* Forecast line is above actual demand; prediction error is consistently positive.\\n\\n*Likely causes*\\n* Holidays/product changes make recent history unrepresentative.\\n* Scheduled-event definitions are too broad (e.g., daily job marked as \\u201chigh\\u201d when it is moderate).\\n* Low-volume workloads where small absolute errors become large relative errors.\\n\\n*Recommended workarounds*\\n1) *Reduce predictive bias* (preferred): switch to \\u201cPredictive + Reactive Override\\u201d (if available in the customer\\u2019s build) or lower the predictive weight via internal config (eng-assisted).\\n2) *Use a tighter max bound* to cap spend if the customer\\u2019s primary concern is budget.\\n3) If customer can tolerate brief queueing, recommend *reactive-only* during the window and re-enable predictive after retraining/after a week of stable traffic.\\n\\n*Support notes*\\n* Collect: deployment_id, region, last 7 days of request rate, and a screenshot of desired vs bounded capacity.\\n* If the customer is in contract negotiation over cost ceilings, steer toward bounds and recommended ranges, not predictive promises.\\n\\nh2. 2) Timezone misalignment (forecast ramps at the wrong local time)\\n*Symptoms*\\n* Customer reports \\u201cit scales for our ramp, but 1\\u20133 hours too early/late.\\u201d\\n* Recurring daily ramp shows a consistent offset.\\n\\n*Likely causes*\\n* Traffic exhibits local-time patterns but the forecast is effectively aligned to UTC (or mis-tagged timezone).\\n* Scheduled events were provided in local time but entered/processed as UTC.\\n\\n*Recommended workarounds*\\n1) Confirm the customer\\u2019s *operational timezone* and the timezone assumed for any scheduled events.\\n2) Temporary mitigation: set a *higher min bound* covering the ramp window until timezone is corrected.\\n3) If the account uses scheduled events: update the event schedule with explicit timezone (eng-assisted if the UI/API does not expose timezone selection yet).\\n\\n*Escalation trigger*\\n* If offset is consistent and reproducible, file an escalation to Eng Infra with: account_id, deployment_id, region, customer timezone, and at least two days of graphs showing the offset.\\n\\nh2. 3) Insufficient history (under-scaling because the predictor lacks training data)\\n*Symptoms*\\n* Predictive mode enabled, but scaling behaves similar to reactive-only.\\n* Forecast confidence is low or \\u201cnot available\\u201d; autoscaler logs indicate fallback to reactive.\\n\\n*Likely causes*\\n* New deployment or new model route without enough steady history.\\n* Major traffic shape change in the last few days.\\n\\n*Recommended workarounds*\\n1) Set a *conservative min bound* aligned to baseline throughput to avoid cold starts.\\n2) Use *reactive-only* for the first 1\\u20132 weeks of a new deployment, then re-enable predictive mode once traffic stabilizes.\\n3) If ramp is known and contractual, use *scheduled events* (if enabled for the account) as an interim signal source.\\n\\n*Support note*\\n* \\u201cPredictive mode\\u201d is not a guarantee; it is a best-effort bias that requires stable patterns.\\n\\nh2. 4) Stale forecast / prediction pipeline outage (sudden behavior change)\\n*Symptoms*\\n* Predictive scaling appears to stop; capacity only changes after queue depth increases.\\n* UI shows forecast timestamp is old, or \\u201cforecast unavailable.\\u201d\\n\\n*Likely causes*\\n* Forecast provider returned stale data; the autoscaler rejected it due to staleness checks.\\n* Regional data pipeline delay.\\n\\n*Recommended workarounds*\\n1) Treat as expected fail-safe: *reactive scaling takes over*.\\n2) Raise min bound temporarily for the affected ramp window.\\n3) If customer is impacted (p95 latency regression), advise disabling predictive mode until pipeline recovers.\\n\\n*Escalation trigger*\\n* Any incident where stale forecasts correlate with user-visible latency/SLO breach: escalate to SRE per the Dedicated autoscaler runbook.\\n\\nh2. 5) Oscillation / capacity jitter (scale up/down thrash)\\n*Symptoms*\\n* Replicas/GPU count changes frequently (e.g., every few minutes).\\n* Customer sees request latency jitter; autoscaler event stream shows alternating scale-up and scale-down.\\n\\n*Likely causes*\\n* Noisy predictions combined with aggressive cooldowns.\\n* Workload has spiky batch traffic that looks like repeated ramps.\\n\\n*Recommended workarounds*\\n1) Increase *cooldown* / dampening parameters (eng-assisted if not customer-configurable yet).\\n2) Increase *min step size* for scale changes (avoid micro-adjustments).\\n3) Prefer reactive signals for scale-down, predictive for scale-up (hybrid mode) where available.\\n4) If the customer is latency-sensitive, disable predictive temporarily and stabilize with min bound.\\n\\n*Support note*\\n* If a pilot customer reports oscillation, check whether they are on the build containing anti-oscillation guardrails. If not, coordinate an upgrade or disable predictive.\\n\\nh2. 6) Null/empty prediction edge case (unsafe downscale risk)\\n*Symptoms*\\n* A forecast response contains null/empty values; desired capacity appears to drop unexpectedly.\\n\\n*Status*\\n* Mitigated by a hotfix to prevent scale-to-zero when predictor returns null. Some older pilot environments may not have the fix.\\n\\n*Recommended workarounds*\\n1) If suspected: disable predictive mode immediately and set min bound to a safe baseline.\\n2) Escalate to Eng Infra with urgency and include timestamps + deployment_id.\\n\\nh2. 7) Max-bound saturation (predictive wants more capacity than allowed)\\n*Symptoms*\\n* Queue depth increases during ramp; customer sees \\u201cwe told it to scale, but it didn\\u2019t.\\u201d\\n* Metrics show frequent *max-bound hit* events.\\n\\n*Likely causes*\\n* The customer\\u2019s max bound is below what the workload requires for the ramp.\\n* Region capacity shortage prevents provisioning even below max (rare but possible).\\n\\n*Recommended workarounds*\\n1) Clarify intent: if max bound is a *hard budget cap*, then queueing is an expected tradeoff.\\n2) If customer goal is SLA/latency, recommend increasing max bound or using burst capacity (if contract allows).\\n3) For predictable ramps: raise min bound ahead of the ramp so the system is already warm.\\n\\n*Escalation trigger*\\n* If min bound cannot be met due to region shortage, treat as a reliability event (see shortage behavior in the runbook).\\n\\nh1. What to ask the customer (minimum checklist)\\n1) Deployment name / deployment_id and region\\n2) Current bounds: min, max, cooldowns (if known)\\n3) Predictive mode state (enabled? hybrid? scheduled events?)\\n4) The customer\\u2019s local timezone and the time window of the ramp\\n5) Impact statement: spend concern vs latency/SLA concern\\n6) Screenshots or exports of: desired vs bounded capacity, queue depth, and p95 latency over the affected window\\n\\nh1. Recommended customer guidance (safe, non-committal language)\\n* \\u201cPredictive autoscaling helps pre-warm capacity for repeating traffic patterns, but it still respects your min/max bounds and will fall back to reactive scaling when forecasts are not available.\\u201d\\n* \\u201cIf the primary goal is controlling spend, set a max bound you\\u2019re comfortable with and we can tune predictive behavior to avoid early ramp-ups.\\u201d\\n* \\u201cIf the primary goal is meeting latency SLO during a known ramp, a higher baseline min (or scheduled event) is often the most reliable first step.\\u201d\\n\\nh1. When to escalate (internal)\\nEscalate to *Eng Infra / SRE* if any of the following are true:\\n* Predictive mode enabled and customer reports sustained latency regression (p95/p99) during a known ramp\\n* Reproducible timezone offset or consistently stale forecasts\\n* Oscillation causing user-visible impact\\n* Suspected null/empty prediction edge case\\n* Min bound cannot be met (possible region shortage)\\n\\nInclude in escalation: account_id, deployment_id, region, timestamps, graphs for queue depth + desired/bounded capacity, and whether disabling predictive mitigates.\\n\\nh1. Changelog\\n* 2025-09-05: Updated mitigations for oscillation and clarified max-bound saturation guidance.\\n* 2025-08-02: Added null/empty prediction edge case and mitigation instructions.\\n* 2025-07-18: Initial publication for pilot support readiness.\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_07daff0e8966460f86c297b6939b607a\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive Autoscaling (Dedicated) — Known Issues & Recommended Workarounds\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/predictive-autoscaling-known-issues.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: customer-success-and-support\n\nconfidentiality : internal body : h1. overview predictive autoscaling is an opt - in mode for * redwood dedicated * that biases scale decisions using forecasted demand ( time - of - day patterns, scheduled events, historical request rates / latency ). predictive mode * does not * override customer - configured * min / max bounds * and will fall back to reactive signals when forecasts are stale / unavailable. this page lists the most common * known issues * observed during pilot / canary, how to recognize them, and recommended * workarounds * for customer success and support. this is not a full runbook ; for deep debugging and mitigations, use the dedicated on - call runbook linked above.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive Autoscaling (Dedicated) — Known Issues & Recommended Workarounds\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/predictive-autoscaling-known-issues.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: customer-success-and-support\n\n- only. * forecast confidence is low or “ not available ” ; autoscaler logs indicate fallback to reactive. * likely causes * * new deployment or new model route without enough steady history. * major traffic shape change in the last few days. * recommended workarounds * 1 ) set a * conservative min bound * aligned to baseline throughput to avoid cold starts. 2 ) use * reactive - only * for the first 1 – 2 weeks of a new deployment, then re - enable predictive mode once traffic stabilizes. 3 ) if ramp is known and contractual, use * scheduled events * ( if enabled for the account ) as an interim signal source.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Predictive Autoscaling (Dedicated) — Known Issues & Recommended Workarounds\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/predictive-autoscaling-known-issues.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: customer-success-and-support\n\n##hots or exports of : desired vs bounded capacity, queue depth, and p95 latency over the affected window h1. recommended customer guidance ( safe, non - committal language ) * “ predictive autoscaling helps pre - warm capacity for repeating traffic patterns, but it still respects your min / max bounds and will fall back to reactive scaling when forecasts are not available. ” * “ if the primary goal is controlling spend, set a max bound you ’ re comfortable with and we can tune predictive behavior to avoid early ramp - ups. ” * “ if the primary goal is meeting latency slo during a known ramp, a higher baseline min ( or scheduled event ) is often the most reliable first step. ”",

document.title: Predictive Autoscaling (Dedicated) — Known Issues & Recommended Workarounds
document.content:
{
  "title": "Predictive Autoscaling (Dedicated) — Known Issues & Recommended Workarounds",
  "space": "customer-success-and-support",
  "author": "Dev Patel",
  "owner_team": "customer-success",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2025-07-18",
  "last_updated": "2025-09-05",
  "reviewers": [
    "Lauren Bishop",
    "Vanessa Ortiz",
    "Rafael Mendes",
    "Allison Grant"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "dedicated",
    "autoscaling",
    "predictive-scaling",
    "known-issues",
    "support-playbook",
    "rollout"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/escalation-playbook/autoscaling-bounds-customer-escalation-playbook.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/dedicated-autoscaler-troubleshooting-runbook.json",
    "sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/autoscaling-bounds-observability-dashboard-spec.json",
    "sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-autoscaling-bounds-precedence-and-safety-invariants.json",
    "sources/confluence/product-docs/release-notes/dedicated-autoscaling-bounds-and-predictive-mode-release-notes.json"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "body": "h1. Overview
Predictive autoscaling is an opt-in mode for *Redwood Dedicated* that biases scale decisions using forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical request rates/latency). Predictive mode *does not* override customer-configured *min/max bounds* and will fall back to reactive signals when forecasts are stale/unavailable.

This page lists the most common *known issues* observed during pilot/canary, how to recognize them, and recommended *workarounds* for Customer Success and Support. This is not a full runbook; for deep debugging and mitigations, use the dedicated on-call runbook linked above.

h2. Scope / When this page applies
* Applies to:* Dedicated deployments with predictive mode enabled (feature-flagged per account/deployment).
* Not applicable to:* Hosted API autoscaling or Dedicated deployments running reactive-only scaling.

h2. Quick definitions (customer-friendly)
* *Forecast / prediction:* A projected target capacity (replicas/GPU slices) for an upcoming time window.
* *Reactive scaling:* Signals like queue depth, saturation, and latency that trigger scaling based on current conditions.
* *Bounds:* Customer-configured *min* and *max* capacity. The autoscaler clamps desired capacity within these bounds.
* *Bound-hit:* When the autoscaler wants to go above max or below min but is prevented by bounds.

h1. Rollout caveats (read first)
1) *Opt-in + guarded rollout:* Predictive mode is still rolling out. Some regions/accounts may not be eligible.
2) *Model/workload sensitivity:* Highly bursty workloads with low steady-state traffic can produce noisy forecasts.
3) *Do not promise “no queueing” under max bounds:* If traffic exceeds max-bound capacity and the region cannot burst, queueing/latency can occur. This is expected behavior; the product surfaces it via bound-hit metrics.
4) *Time-to-effect:* Changes to predictive settings may take up to *10–20 minutes* to reflect in decisions (depending on caching and evaluation intervals).

h1. Known issues & workarounds

h2. 1) False positives (over-scaling before traffic arrives)
*Symptoms*
* Capacity ramps up early; customer sees increased spend/idle utilization.
* Forecast line is above actual demand; prediction error is consistently positive.

*Likely causes*
* Holidays/product changes make recent history unrepresentative.
* Scheduled-event definitions are too broad (e.g., daily job marked as “high” when it is moderate).
* Low-volume workloads where small absolute errors become large relative errors.

*Recommended workarounds*
1) *Reduce predictive bias* (preferred): switch to “Predictive + Reactive Override” (if available in the customer’s build) or lower the predictive weight via internal config (eng-assisted).
2) *Use a tighter max bound* to cap spend if the customer’s primary concern is budget.
3) If customer can tolerate brief queueing, recommend *reactive-only* during the window and re-enable predictive after retraining/after a week of stable traffic.

*Support notes*
* Collect: deployment_id, region, last 7 days of request rate, and a screenshot of desired vs bounded capacity.
* If the customer is in contract negotiation over cost ceilings, steer toward bounds and recommended ranges, not predictive promises.

h2. 2) Timezone misalignment (forecast ramps at the wrong local time)
*Symptoms*
* Customer reports “it scales for our ramp, but 1–3 hours too early/late.”
* Recurring daily ramp shows a consistent offset.

*Likely causes*
* Traffic exhibits local-time patterns but the forecast is effectively aligned to UTC (or mis-tagged timezone).
* Scheduled events were provided in local time but entered/processed as UTC.

*Recommended workarounds*
1) Confirm the customer’s *operational timezone* and the timezone assumed for any scheduled events.
2) Temporary mitigation: set a *higher min bound* covering the ramp window until timezone is corrected.
3) If the account uses scheduled events: update the event schedule with explicit timezone (eng-assisted if the UI/API does not expose timezone selection yet).

*Escalation trigger*
* If offset is consistent and reproducible, file an escalation to Eng Infra with: account_id, deployment_id, region, customer timezone, and at least two days of graphs showing the offset.

h2. 3) Insufficient history (under-scaling because the predictor lacks training data)
*Symptoms*
* Predictive mode enabled, but scaling behaves similar to reactive-only.
* Forecast confidence is low or “not available”; autoscaler logs indicate fallback to reactive.

*Likely causes*
* New deployment or new model route without enough steady history.
* Major traffic shape change in the last few days.

*Recommended workarounds*
1) Set a *conservative min bound* aligned to baseline throughput to avoid cold starts.
2) Use *reactive-only* for the first 1–2 weeks of a new deployment, then re-enable predictive mode once traffic stabilizes.
3) If ramp is known and contractual, use *scheduled events* (if enabled for the account) as an interim signal source.

*Support note*
* “Predictive mode” is not a guarantee; it is a best-effort bias that requires stable patterns.

h2. 4) Stale forecast / prediction pipeline outage (sudden behavior change)
*Symptoms*
* Predictive scaling appears to stop; capacity only changes after queue depth increases.
* UI shows forecast timestamp is old, or “forecast unavailable.”

*Likely causes*
* Forecast provider returned stale data; the autoscaler rejected it due to staleness checks.
* Regional data pipeline delay.

*Recommended workarounds*
1) Treat as expected fail-safe: *reactive scaling takes over*.
2) Raise min bound temporarily for the affected ramp window.
3) If customer is impacted (p95 latency regression), advise disabling predictive mode until pipeline recovers.

*Escalation trigger*
* Any incident where stale forecasts correlate with user-visible latency/SLO breach: escalate to SRE per the Dedicated autoscaler runbook.

h2. 5) Oscillation / capacity jitter (scale up/down thrash)
*Symptoms*
* Replicas/GPU count changes frequently (e.g., every few minutes).
* Customer sees request latency jitter; autoscaler event stream shows alternating scale-up and scale-down.

*Likely causes*
* Noisy predictions combined with aggressive cooldowns.
* Workload has spiky batch traffic that looks like repeated ramps.

*Recommended workarounds*
1) Increase *cooldown* / dampening parameters (eng-assisted if not customer-configurable yet).
2) Increase *min step size* for scale changes (avoid micro-adjustments).
3) Prefer reactive signals for scale-down, predictive for scale-up (hybrid mode) where available.
4) If the customer is latency-sensitive, disable predictive temporarily and stabilize with min bound.

*Support note*
* If a pilot customer reports oscillation, check whether they are on the build containing anti-oscillation guardrails. If not, coordinate an upgrade or disable predictive.

h2. 6) Null/empty prediction edge case (unsafe downscale risk)
*Symptoms*
* A forecast response contains null/empty values; desired capacity appears to drop unexpectedly.

*Status*
* Mitigated by a hotfix to prevent scale-to-zero when predictor returns null. Some older pilot environments may not have the fix.

*Recommended workarounds*
1) If suspected: disable predictive mode immediately and set min bound to a safe baseline.
2) Escalate to Eng Infra with urgency and include timestamps + deployment_id.

h2. 7) Max-bound saturation (predictive wants more capacity than allowed)
*Symptoms*
* Queue depth increases during ramp; customer sees “we told it to scale, but it didn’t.”
* Metrics show frequent *max-bound hit* events.

*Likely causes*
* The customer’s max bound is below what the workload requires for the ramp.
* Region capacity shortage prevents provisioning even below max (rare but possible).

*Recommended workarounds*
1) Clarify intent: if max bound is a *hard budget cap*, then queueing is an expected tradeoff.
2) If customer goal is SLA/latency, recommend increasing max bound or using burst capacity (if contract allows).
3) For predictable ramps: raise min bound ahead of the ramp so the system is already warm.

*Escalation trigger*
* If min bound cannot be met due to region shortage, treat as a reliability event (see shortage behavior in the runbook).

h1. What to ask the customer (minimum checklist)
1) Deployment name / deployment_id and region
2) Current bounds: min, max, cooldowns (if known)
3) Predictive mode state (enabled? hybrid? scheduled events?)
4) The customer’s local timezone and the time window of the ramp
5) Impact statement: spend concern vs latency/SLA concern
6) Screenshots or exports of: desired vs bounded capacity, queue depth, and p95 latency over the affected window

h1. Recommended customer guidance (safe, non-committal language)
* “Predictive autoscaling helps pre-warm capacity for repeating traffic patterns, but it still respects your min/max bounds and will fall back to reactive scaling when forecasts are not available.”
* “If the primary goal is controlling spend, set a max bound you’re comfortable with and we can tune predictive behavior to avoid early ramp-ups.”
* “If the primary goal is meeting latency SLO during a known ramp, a higher baseline min (or scheduled event) is often the most reliable first step.”

h1. When to escalate (internal)
Escalate to *Eng Infra / SRE* if any of the following are true:
* Predictive mode enabled and customer reports sustained latency regression (p95/p99) during a known ramp
* Reproducible timezone offset or consistently stale forecasts
* Oscillation causing user-visible impact
* Suspected null/empty prediction edge case
* Min bound cannot be met (possible region shortage)

Include in escalation: account_id, deployment_id, region, timestamps, graphs for queue depth + desired/bounded capacity, and whether disabling predictive mitigates.

h1. Changelog
* 2025-09-05: Updated mitigations for oscillation and clarified max-bound saturation guidance.
* 2025-08-02: Added null/empty prediction edge case and mitigation instructions.
* 2025-07-18: Initial publication for pilot support readiness.",

    "title": "Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/linear",
    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"ENG-428317\",\n  \"team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"title\": \"Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement\",\n  \"status\": \"In Progress\",\n  \"priority\": \"P1\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-12\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-03-14\",\n  \"creator\": \"Lina Chen\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Marco Ruiz\",\n  \"project\": \"RateEngine 2.0 - correctness\",\n  \"cycle\": \"2026-Q1-Cycle 5\",\n  \"estimate\": \"5\",\n  \"due_date\": \"2026-03-21\",\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"billing\",\n    \"rate-limiter\",\n    \"investigation\",\n    \"high-impact\"\n  ],\n  \"description\": \"Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.\",\n  \"reproduction_steps\": [\n    \"1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).\",\n    \"2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.\",\n    \"3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.\",\n    \"4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.\",\n    \"5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.\",\n    \"6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.\",\n    \"7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads.\"\n  ],\n  \"impact\": \"Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.\",\n  \"customer_impact\": \"medium\",\n  \"logs_snapshot\": [\n    \"edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z\",\n    \"shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27\",\n    \"policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled\",\n    \"meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200\"\n  ],\n  \"hypothesis\": \"A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.\",\n  \"experiment_results\": \"Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.\",\n  \"root_cause\": \"Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.\",\n  \"mitigations\": \"Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.\",\n  \"rollout_plan\": \"1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.\",\n  \"long_term_fix\": \"Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.\",\n  \"regression_test_plan\": \"Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.\",\n  \"dependencies\": [\n    \"ENG-430001 (shard-handoff-stabilization)\",\n    \"ENG-429112 (policy-hot-reload-atomicity)\",\n    \"ENG-421007 (prefetch-credit-tombstone-investigation)\"\n  ],\n  \"links\": [\n    \"https://confluence.redwood/inference/rateengine-2.0/priority-pointer-design\",\n    \"https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/8523 (staging short-term patch)\",\n    \"https://grafana.redwood/board/edge-allow-spikes?from=now-1d&org=tenant\",\n    \"s3://redwood-logs/2026-03-12/shard-hand-off-traces.tar.gz\"\n  ],\n  \"notes\": [\n    \"PM (Aisha Kapoor): prioritize mitigation; billing reconciliation may be needed if misapplied credits persist beyond 24h.\",\n    \"Security (Rajiv Patel): no PII involved in pointers but ensure tracing does not expose tenant ids in public dashboards.\",\n    \"Observation: reproduces more reliably when policy reload contains route fallback toggles rather than pure priority edits.\"\n  ],\n  \"release\": \"rateengine-2.0.3\",\n  \"security_review_required\": \"false\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"impact\",\n    \"reproduction_steps\",\n    \"logs_snapshot\",\n    \"hypothesis\",\n    \"experiment_results\",\n    \"root_cause\",\n    \"mitigations\",\n    \"rollout_plan\",\n    \"long_term_fix\",\n    \"regression_test_plan\",\n    \"notes\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: RateEngine 2.0 - correctness\nTeam: engineering\n\nenforcement uses the fast - path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur. experiment results : replayed the sequence in staging using the shard - reassign harness. with no policy reload the issue did not occur. when timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over - allow consistently. enabling stronger pointer validation ( temporary patch ) eliminated the over - allows in the harness.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: RateEngine 2.0 - correctness\nTeam: engineering\n\nreproduced the over - allow consistently. enabling stronger pointer validation ( temporary patch ) eliminated the over - allows in the harness. root cause : sticky - shard pointer ( in - memory bucket reference ) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast - path credit application. policy hot - reload mutates the route / priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers ; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant ' s bucket. enforcement fast - path accepts the cache without full tenant - level validation.",

document.title: Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement
document.content:
{
  "key": "ENG-428317",
  "team": "engineering",
  "title": "Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement",
  "status": "In Progress",
  "priority": "P1",
  "created_at": "2026-03-12",
  "updated_at": "2026-03-14",
  "creator": "Lina Chen",
  "assignee": "Marco Ruiz",
  "project": "RateEngine 2.0 - correctness",
  "cycle": "2026-Q1-Cycle 5",
  "estimate": "5",
  "due_date": "2026-03-21",
  "labels": [
    "billing",
    "rate-limiter",
    "investigation",
    "high-impact"
  ],
  "description": "Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.",
  "reproduction_steps": [
    "1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).",
    "2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.",
    "3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.",
    "4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.",
    "5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.",
    "6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.",
    "7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads."
  ],
  "impact": "Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.",
  "customer_impact": "medium",
  "logs_snapshot": [
    "edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z",
    "shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27",
    "policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled",
    "meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200"
  ],
  "hypothesis": "A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.",
  "experiment_results": "Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.",
  "root_cause": "Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.",
  "mitigations": "Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.",
  "rollout_plan": "1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.",
  "long_term_fix": "Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.",
  "regression_test_plan": "Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.",
  "dependencies": [
    "ENG-430001 (shard-handoff-stabilization)",
    "ENG-429112 (policy-hot-reload-atomicity)",
    "ENG-421007 (prefetch-credit-tombstone-investigation)"
  ],
  "links": [
    "https://confluence.redwood/inference/rateengine-2.0/priority-pointer-design",
    "https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/8523 (staging short-term patch)",
    "https://grafana.redwood/board/edge-allow-spikes?from=now-1d&org=tenant",
    "s3://redwood-logs/2026-03-12/shard-hand-off-traces.tar.gz"
  ],
  "notes": [
    "PM (Aisha Kapoor): prioritize mitigation; billing reconciliation may be needed if misapplied credits persist beyond 24h.",
    "Security (Rajiv Patel): no PII involved in pointers but ensure tracing does not expose tenant ids in public dashboards.",
    "Observation: reproduces more reliably when policy reload contains route fallback toggles rather than pure priority edits."
  ],
  "release": "rateengine-2.0.3",
  "security_review_required": "false",
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "description",

    "experiment_results",
    "root_cause",

    "rollout_plan",
    "long_term_fix",
    "regression_test_plan",
    "notes"
  ],

}

# Cross-language streaming startup hang

## Symptom
Long-running streaming sessions can stall during startup/shutdown-adjacent token refresh, with language-dependent behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go. The supported signature is a stream drain that does not complete when refresh overlaps EOF or cancellation.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative merged SDK change identifies two coupled causes: inconsistent session grace defaults (Python 5s, TypeScript 2s, Go none) and nondeterministic consumer drain logic. # Predictive autoscaling reacts too late to known load

## Symptom
A known demand ramp arrives before dedicated capacity is usable, producing queue growth and p95/p99 latency even though predictive scaling is enabled.

## Diagnosis
The supported leading diagnosis is insufficient predictive lead time relative to GPU provisioning/warmup: ENG-22142 explicitly flags the 10-minute default as potentially too low for some SKUs and regions. “Known load” alone does not prove the forecast was timely; distinguish a correctly timed scale decision with late readiness from timezone offset, stale/null forecast, max-bound clamping, conservative cooldown, or regional shortage.

## Reproduction / validation
For the affected deployment, align in UTC: scheduled ramp, forecast timestamp/freshness, predictive scale decision, desired versus bounded replicas, node/model readiness, queue depth, and p95 latency. Reproduce with a synthetic daily ramp and a fake forecast provider. Diagnosis is confirmed when the prediction and scale-up request precede the ramp but usable capacity arrives after it, and increasing prewarm lead/minimum capacity removes queueing. A consistent 1–3 hour offset instead indicates timezone handling.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum bound for a window beginning earlier than the measured provisioning-plus-warmup p95 and ensure the max bound permits the forecasted capacity. Increase predictive lead time for the affected SKU/region. These changes are reversible after validation; if forecasts are stale or oscillatory, disable predictive for the deployment and use scheduled minimum capacity while reactive safety behavior remains.

## Uncertainty
No deployment timeline or region/SKU metrics were supplied, so lead-time insufficiency is a supported diagnosis, not a confirmed incident-specific root cause. Validate timezone, forecast freshness, bounds, cooldown/step sizing, and regional availability before closure.

## Evidence
- `dsid_af8cb184a4ed4eed8e547015f0933e00` — `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-22142-predictive-signal-ingestion-and-forecast-interface.json`

# Incorrect throttling during overlapping shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
During concurrent sticky-shard reassignment and policy hot reload, requests can be transiently over-allowed (and therefore incorrectly throttled relative to the intended tenant policy), especially with per-key overrides/burst credits and route fallback changes.

## Diagnosis
ENG-428317 provides a deterministic root cause: the fast-path cached credit pointer was validated by shard ID but not tenant ID. Policy reload mutates route/priority indices while shard transfer copies pointers, permitting a transient pointer to another tenant’s credit bucket. The fast path then applies the wrong credits. This is distinct from epoch-compaction debit loss and metering dual-write races.

## Reproduction / validation
In the runtime-policy simulator, concurrently trigger sticky-shard handoff and policy hot reload while applying per-key overrides and burst credits; route fallback toggles raise reproduction probability. Capture tenant, shard, key, target bucket, and decision. The documented harness reproduced over-allows consistently; enabling tenant-ID pointer validation eliminated them. Validate canary telemetry with no over-allow traces, then run deterministic concurrency, property, randomized rolling-update, and accounting reconciliation checks.

## Reversible mitigation
Enable tenant-ID validation on every fast-path cached credit pointer before credit application and lengthen shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Roll out by low-traffic canary with trace sampling, then ramp gradually; rollback the patch if latency or correctness regresses. As an operational containment, serialize policy reloads and shard reassignments for affected fleets until the immutable namespaced pointer/versioned-binder fix is deployed.

## Uncertainty
The authoritative ticket remains In Progress and records canary/partial-rollout status, not proof of fleet-wide remediation. Historical accounting impact requires reconciliation. If the observed symptom is double-throttling rather than over-allow, test the separate reservation/coalescer paths instead of forcing this diagnosis.

## Evidence
- `dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93` — `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json`

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: cross-language streaming startup hang\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/cross-language-streaming-startup-hang.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-streaming-startup-hang\n\n# Cross-language streaming startup hang\n\n## Symptom\nLong-running streaming sessions can stall during startup/shutdown-adjacent token refresh, with language-dependent behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go. The supported signature is a stream drain that does not complete when refresh overlaps EOF or cancellation.\n\n## Diagnosis\nThe authoritative merged SDK change identifies two coupled causes: inconsistent session grace defaults (Python 5s, TypeScript 2s, Go none) and nondeterministic consumer drain logic. When token refresh overlaps generation/EOF, refresh and drain contend; prior refresh handling did not reliably yield shutdown precedence. A separate Go reproduction records request-context reuse by background auth refresh (“context bleed”), so cancellation stops refresh and leaves the reconnect/retry path stalled. This is an SDK lifecycle defect, not evidence of a server-capacity failure.\n\n## Reproduction / validation\nUse the cross-SDK concurrent-refresh-and-EOF stress harness referenced by PR 405999, or inject a slow token refresh while starting/canceling a stream. Validate the fix with Python/TS/Go integration tests and confirm bounded exit, no goroutine/task leak, and metrics `sdk.refresh.yield_to_drain`, `sdk.session.grace_ms_applied`, and `sdk.stream.drain_timeout_ms_applied`. PR CI passed cross-SDK and perf-harness coverage after a TypeScript drain-signal race was corrected.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nPrefer SDKs containing PR 405999 behavior (Python 1.9.0, TypeScript 2.6.1, Go 1.4.0). Configure canonical `session_grace_ms=5000` and `stream_drain_timeout_ms=3000`; keep refresh cancellation separate from the request/stream context. If shutdown latency regresses, revert to prior per-SDK grace values while retaining an explicit bounded drain and roll back the canary.\n\n## Uncertainty\nThe evidence strongly supports refresh/drain contention for this signature, but the production report lacks SDK versions, exact phase (before first byte versus shutdown), and context traces. An idle connection after bytes stop may instead be the distinct streaming-idle-timeout issue; confirm refresh/EOF overlap before declaring this diagnosis.",

# Cross-language streaming startup hang

## Symptom
Long-running streaming sessions can stall during startup/shutdown-adjacent token refresh, with language-dependent behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go. The supported signature is a stream drain that does not complete when refresh overlaps EOF or cancellation.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative merged SDK change identifies two coupled causes: inconsistent session grace defaults (Python 5s, TypeScript 2s, Go none) and nondeterministic consumer drain logic. When token refresh overlaps generation/EOF, refresh and drain contend; prior refresh handling did not reliably yield shutdown precedence. A separate Go reproduction records request-context reuse by background auth refresh (“context bleed”), so cancellation stops refresh and leaves the reconnect/retry path stalled. This is an SDK lifecycle defect, not evidence of a server-capacity failure.

## Reproduction / validation
Use the cross-SDK concurrent-refresh-and-EOF stress harness referenced by PR 405999, or inject a slow token refresh while starting/canceling a stream. Validate the fix with Python/TS/Go integration tests and confirm bounded exit, no goroutine/task leak, and metrics `sdk.refresh.yield_to_drain`, `sdk.session.grace_ms_applied`, and `sdk.stream.drain_timeout_ms_applied`. PR CI passed cross-SDK and perf-harness coverage after a TypeScript drain-signal race was corrected.

## Reversible mitigation
Prefer SDKs containing PR 405999 behavior (Python 1.9.0, TypeScript 2.6.1, Go 1.4.0). Configure canonical `session_grace_ms=5000` and `stream_drain_timeout_ms=3000`; keep refresh cancellation separate from the request/stream context. If shutdown latency regresses, revert to prior per-SDK grace values while retaining an explicit bounded drain and roll back the canary.

## Uncertainty
The evidence strongly supports refresh/drain contention for this signature, but the production report lacks SDK versions, exact phase (before first byte versus shutdown), and context traces. An idle connection after bytes stop may instead be the distinct streaming-idle-timeout issue; confirm refresh/EOF overlap before declaring this diagnosis.

# Predictive autoscaling reacts too late to known load

## Symptom
A known demand ramp arrives before dedicated capacity is usable, producing queue growth and p95/p99 latency even though predictive scaling is enabled.

## Diagnosis
The supported leading diagnosis is insufficient predictive lead time relative to GPU provisioning/warmup: ENG-22142 explicitly flags the 10-minute default as potentially too low for some SKUs and regions. “Known load” alone does not prove the forecast was timely; distinguish a correctly timed scale decision with late readiness from timezone offset, stale/null forecast, max-bound clamping, conservative cooldown, or regional shortage.

## Reproduction / validation
For the affected deployment, align in UTC: scheduled ramp, forecast timestamp/freshness, predictive scale decision, desired versus bounded replicas, node/model readiness, queue depth, and p95 latency. Reproduce with a synthetic daily ramp and a fake forecast provider. Diagnosis is confirmed when the prediction and scale-up request precede the ramp but usable capacity arrives after it, and increasing prewarm lead/minimum capacity removes queueing. A consistent 1–3 hour offset instead indicates timezone handling.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum bound for a window beginning earlier than the measured provisioning-plus-warmup p95 and ensure the max bound permits the forecasted capacity. Increase predictive lead time for the affected SKU/region. These changes are reversible after validation; if forecasts are stale or oscillatory, disable predictive for the deployment and use scheduled minimum capacity while reactive safety behavior remains.

## Uncertainty
No deployment timeline or region/SKU metrics were supplied, so lead-time insufficiency is a supported diagnosis, not a confirmed incident-specific root cause. Validate timezone, forecast freshness, bounds, cooldown/step sizing, and regional availability before closure.

# Incorrect throttling during overlapping shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
During concurrent sticky-shard reassignment and policy hot reload, requests can be transiently over-allowed (and therefore incorrectly throttled relative to the intended tenant policy), especially with per-key overrides/burst credits and route fallback changes.

## Diagnosis
ENG-428317 provides a deterministic root cause: the fast-path cached credit pointer was validated by shard ID but not tenant ID. Policy reload mutates route/priority indices while shard transfer copies pointers, permitting a transient pointer to another tenant’s credit bucket. The fast path then applies the wrong credits. This is distinct from epoch-compaction debit loss and metering dual-write races.

## Reproduction / validation
In the runtime-policy simulator, concurrently trigger sticky-shard handoff and policy hot reload while applying per-key overrides and burst credits; route fallback toggles raise reproduction probability. # Incorrect throttling during overlapping shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
During concurrent sticky-shard reassignment and policy hot reload, requests can be transiently over-allowed (and therefore incorrectly throttled relative to the intended tenant policy), especially with per-key overrides/burst credits and route fallback changes.

## Diagnosis
ENG-428317 provides a deterministic root cause: the fast-path cached credit pointer was validated by shard ID but not tenant ID. Policy reload mutates route/priority indices while shard transfer copies pointers, permitting a transient pointer to another tenant’s credit bucket. The fast path then applies the wrong credits. This is distinct from epoch-compaction debit loss and metering dual-write races.

## Reproduction / validation
In the runtime-policy simulator, concurrently trigger sticky-shard handoff and policy hot reload while applying per-key overrides and burst credits; route fallback toggles raise reproduction probability. Capture tenant, shard, key, target bucket, and decision. The documented harness reproduced over-allows consistently; enabling tenant-ID pointer validation eliminated them. Validate canary telemetry with no over-allow traces, then run deterministic concurrency, property, randomized rolling-update, and accounting reconciliation checks.

## Reversible mitigation
Enable tenant-ID validation on every fast-path cached credit pointer before credit application and lengthen shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Roll out by low-traffic canary with trace sampling, then ramp gradually; rollback the patch if latency or correctness regresses. As an operational containment, serialize policy reloads and shard reassignments for affected fleets until the immutable namespaced pointer/versioned-binder fix is deployed.

## Uncertainty
The authoritative ticket remains In Progress and records canary/partial-rollout status, not proof of fleet-wide remediation. Historical accounting impact requires reconciliation.
